fields.title: The Pursuit of God (For Teens)
fields.description: A. W. Tozer never went to high school, yet he spent hours lying face-down on his study floor in Chicago, simply gazing at God. Out of that hunger came The Pursuit of God (1948), a short book that has been read by Christians ever since. Its ten chapters call believers beyond knowing about God to actually knowing him, and each one ends with a prayer: “I want to want Thee.” This teen edition follows Tozer chapter by chapter, keeps his prayers in his own words, and asks what pursuing God looks like in a life full of noise, comparison and screens.

qa.question: Who was A. W. Tozer?
qa.answer: Aiden Wilson Tozer (1897–1963) was an American pastor, born near La Jose in western Pennsylvania. He never went to high school, college or seminary and taught himself from libraries and second-hand bookshops. He became a Christian at about seventeen in Akron, Ohio, was ordained in the Christian and Missionary Alliance in 1920, and pastored Southside Alliance Church in Chicago for thirty-one years before moving to Toronto, where he died in 1963.

qa.question: What does “the pursuit of God” mean?
qa.answer: It means going on to know God himself, as a person, not just believing the right things about him. Tozer taught that becoming a Christian is “not an end but an inception”: the start of a lifelong friendship. God starts the pursuit by drawing us, and we respond by seeking him, the way a psalm says, “My soul followeth hard after thee.”

qa.question: What is the original book, and when and why was it written?
qa.answer: The Pursuit of God is a short book of ten chapters, each ending with a prayer, published in 1948 while Tozer was a pastor in Chicago. He wrote it because he saw many Christians with correct beliefs but little real experience of God, and a growing number who were hungry for “God Himself.” He called it “a modest attempt to aid God's hungry children so to find Him.”

qa.question: Is this edition honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It keeps Tozer's blunt criticism of the churches of his day, his use of the disturbing story of Abraham and Isaac, and his insistence that letting God deal with our selfishness hurts. It also says plainly that, according to his biographers, his absorption in God made him distant from his wife and seven children.

qa.question: What does “I want to want Thee” mean?
qa.answer: It comes from the prayer at the end of Tozer's first chapter. He admits he is “ashamed of my lack of desire” for God, and instead of pretending, he asks God to make him want more. It means you don't have to feel on fire for God to begin: you can start by asking God to give you the desire.

qa.question: Did Tozer really write the book in one night on a train?
qa.answer: His biographers report that he drafted much of it in a single night on a train journey to Texas. Its introduction, by Samuel M. Zwemer, says it was the result of long meditation and much prayer. Both can be true: the writing may have come quickly because the thinking and praying had gone on for years.

qa.question: How does Tozer speak about other Christians?
qa.answer: He can be sharp about shallow faith, entertainment in church and self-promoting leaders. But he says “I trust I speak in charity,” includes himself in the blame (“We have all contributed”), and admits when an idea is only his opinion: “you can be a good Christian and not accept my thesis.”

qa.question: What can a teenager take from it?
qa.answer: That being hungry for God is a good sign, not a problem; that God is always present, even when we don't notice; that faith is simply looking to Jesus, even when your mind wanders; that you can stop pretending and comparing; and that ordinary things like homework, chores and time with family can be done as worship.

fields.title: A Fire Not Large, but Real
fields.body_html:
“And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.” — Jeremiah 29:13 (KJV)

In 1948 a Chicago pastor named A. W. Tozer published a short book with a huge hunger inside it. He was born on 21 April 1897 near La Jose, in rural western Pennsylvania. He never sat in a high school classroom or a seminary. He taught himself from libraries and second-hand bookshops.

When he was about seventeen, walking home in Akron, Ohio, he heard a street preacher urging people to call on God for mercy. He went home, up to the attic, and gave his life to Christ. In 1918 he married Ada Cecelia Pfautz, and in 1920 he was ordained in the Christian and Missionary Alliance without a single formal qualification. In 1928 he came to Southside Alliance Church in Chicago, and he stayed for thirty-one years.

He often prayed lying face-down on his study floor, sometimes for hours, simply gazing at God and worshipping. The Pursuit of God grew out of that hunger. His biographers also do not hide something harder: the same absorption made him distant from his wife and their seven children. We will come back to that at the end.

Samuel M. Zwemer, who wrote the book's introduction, could hardly believe a book like this had come from “a busy pastor in Chicago,” in a small study on that “vast, flat checker-board of endless streets.” He had visited Tozer's church and found “a self-made scholar” who “seemed to burn the midnight oil in pursuit of God.” He noticed that every chapter ends with a prayer. Those prayers, he said, “are for closet, not pulpit,” meaning they are for praying alone, not for performing in public. “I felt the nearness of God while reading them.”

Tozer's own preface explains why he wrote. Among ordinary Christians there were “increasing numbers of persons whose religious lives are marked by a growing hunger after God Himself.” These people “will not be put off with words.” In his words, “They are athirst for God, and they will not be satisfied till they have drunk deep at the Fountain of Living Water.”

He was also worried. He borrowed the story of Elijah on Mount Carmel, where God sent fire on the altar. Many churches, he said, had built the altar and laid out the sacrifice, “but now seems satisfied to count the stones and rearrange the pieces with never a care that there is not a sign of fire upon the top of lofty Carmel.” That is blunt, but he adds, “I trust I speak in charity,” and what he feels is sadness: “It is a solemn thing, and no small scandal in the Kingdom, to see God's children starving while actually seated at the Father's table.”

His main point is simple. “For it is not mere words that nourish the soul, but God Himself.” The Bible matters enormously to him, but it is “not an end in itself, but a means to bring men to an intimate and satisfying knowledge of God.” Then he ends with a sentence that is almost shy:

“This book is a modest attempt to aid God's hungry children so to find Him. Nothing here is new except in the sense that it is a discovery which my own heart has made of spiritual realities most delightful and wonderful to me. Others before me have gone much farther into these holy mysteries than I have done, but if my fire is not large it is yet real, and there may be those who can light their candle at its flame.”

This book follows Tozer's ten chapters in order and keeps his prayers in his words. You might know a lot about God already: Bible verses, church, youth group, the right answers. And you might still feel strangely hungry. Tozer would say that hunger is the best sign there is. It means God is drawing you toward himself and not just toward facts about him.

One thing to do this week: finish this sentence honestly, in writing, and keep it somewhere you will see it again: What I actually want from God is... Don't make it sound good. Make it true. You will come back to it at the end of this book.

study_questions.question: How did A. W. Tozer get his education?
study_questions.answer: He taught himself. He never went to high school, college or seminary, but read everything he could find in libraries and second-hand bookshops.

study_questions.question: What did Tozer mean by Christians “starving while actually seated at the Father's table”?
study_questions.answer: That many Christians had plenty of correct teaching about God but were not actually being fed by God himself, because words alone do not nourish the soul.

study_questions.question: Why does Tozer call his fire “not large” but “real”?
study_questions.answer: He was being humble: others had gone further with God than he had. But what he had found was real, and he hoped others could light their own candle from it.

fields.title: I Want to Want Thee
fields.body_html:
“My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me.” — Psalm 63:8 (KJV)

Tozer's first chapter starts with a surprise. You might think the pursuit of God begins with us. It doesn't. “Before a man can seek God, God must first have sought the man.” The very wish to look for God is something God puts in you. “We pursue God because, and only because, He has first put an urge within us that spurs us to the pursuit.” As an old writer, von Hügel, put it: “God is always previous.”

That doesn't make us passive. God starts it, but we must respond. Tozer worried that becoming a Christian had been made to feel like a box ticked. “Christ may be 'received' without creating any special love for Him in the soul of the receiver. The man is 'saved,' but he is not hungry nor thirsty after God.” Worse, people were told to be content with that.

His most famous line in this chapter is this: “The modern scientist has lost God amid the wonders of His world; we Christians are in real danger of losing God amid the wonders of His Word.” You can know your Bible well and still treat God as a subject instead of a person. “We have almost forgotten that God is a Person and, as such, can be cultivated as any person can.” Think about friendship. Nobody becomes a best friend in one conversation. As Tozer says, “full knowledge of one personality by another cannot be achieved in one encounter.”

So finding God is not the end. “It is, however, not an end but an inception, for now begins the glorious pursuit.” He calls this “the soul's paradox of love”: “To have found God and still to pursue Him.” Moses already knew God, yet he asked for more: “I beseech thee, show me thy glory.”

Then comes one of Tozer's sharpest sentences. Jesus, he says, wants to be wanted. “He waits to be wanted. Too bad that with many of us He waits so long, so very long, in vain.” Instead, we keep busy. He saw churches full of “programs, methods, organizations and a world of nervous activities which occupy time and attention but can never satisfy the longing of the heart.”

His answer is to simplify. The problem is the habit of seeking God plus something else. “In the 'and' lies our great woe.” He quotes an old English book called The Cloud of Unknowing, which advises that when you pray, you pick one short word to hold on to: “And such a word is this word GOD or this word LOVE.” God told the tribe of Levi, who got no land, “I am thy part and thine inheritance.” “The man who has God for his treasure has all things in One.”

Then Tozer prays. Notice how honest it is. He does not claim to be full of desire for God. He admits he isn't, and asks God to make him want more:

“O God, I have tasted Thy goodness, and it has both satisfied me and made me thirsty for more. I am painfully conscious of my need of further grace. I am ashamed of my lack of desire. O God, the Triune God, I want to want Thee; I long to be filled with longing; I thirst to be made more thirsty still. Show me Thy glory, I pray Thee, that so I may know Thee indeed.”

Here is the good news hidden in that prayer. You don't have to feel on fire for God to start. You can start where Tozer did: “I want to want Thee.” If you can honestly say even that much, God is already drawing you, because, remember, he is always previous.

And watch for your own “and.” God and good grades. God and being liked. God and a future that goes exactly to plan. None of those things is bad. The trouble comes when God is one item on the list instead of the one you are actually looking for.

One thing to do this week: each morning this week, before you check your phone, pray Tozer's shortest line in your own words: God, I want to want you. Just that. Then notice, by Sunday, whether anything in you has changed.

study_questions.question: What does Tozer mean by “God is always previous”?
study_questions.answer: That God always moves first. Even our wish to look for God is something he put in us before we started looking.

study_questions.question: What is the “paradox of love” in this chapter?
study_questions.answer: Having found God and still wanting to pursue him further, the way Moses knew God and still asked to see his glory.

study_questions.question: Why does Tozer say “In the 'and' lies our great woe”?
study_questions.answer: Because the habit of seeking God plus something else keeps us from finding God fully. If we drop the extra thing we want alongside him, we find him.

fields.title: My Coward Heart
fields.body_html:
“Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 5:3 (KJV)

Tozer's second chapter is about stuff, and something deeper. When God made people, he surrounded them with good gifts, which Genesis simply calls “things.” Those things were meant to stay outside us. “In the deep heart of the man was a shrine where none but God was worthy to come.”

Sin changed that. Now the things have moved inside. Tozer says there is “a tough fibrous root of fallen life whose nature is to possess, always to possess.” Listen to how often you say two small words: “The pronouns 'my' and 'mine' look innocent enough in print, but their constant and universal use is significant.” The result is upside down: “God's gifts now take the place of God.”

Tozer calls this grabbing enemy inside us “the self-life,” and says it is beaten not by fighting harder but by surrendering. That is what Jesus meant by “the poor in spirit.” The word “poor,” Tozer explains, pictures “the common beggar in the streets of Jerusalem”: someone who holds on to nothing.

To show what this looks like, Tozer tells one of the hardest stories in the Bible. Abraham waited until he was old to have a son, Isaac, and loved him so much that the boy became “the delight and idol of his heart.” Then God told Abraham to take Isaac up a mountain and offer him as a sacrifice. It is a disturbing story, and Tozer doesn't pretend otherwise. He imagines the old man that night, “the bent form and convulsive wrestling alone under the stars.” By morning Abraham had decided to obey and to trust God to raise his son from the dead.

God stopped him before he harmed the boy. Tozer imagines God saying to Abraham, “in effect”: “I never intended that you should actually slay the lad. I only wanted to remove him from the temple of your heart that I might reign unchallenged there.” Abraham went home with Isaac alive and well, and Tozer's summary is one of the best lines in the book: “He had everything, but he possessed nothing. There is the spiritual secret.”

Abraham didn't lose his son. He lost his grip. Tozer adds a promise for anyone scared to let go of people they love: “Everything is safe which we commit to Him, and nothing is really safe which is not so committed.” The same goes for our talents: “We have no more right to claim credit for special abilities than for blue eyes or strong muscles.”

What should we do? First, stop making excuses. “Whoever defends himself will have himself for his defense, and he will have no other.” Then get specific: “It may be he will need to become specific, to name things and people by their names one by one.” Tozer is honest that this hurts, like a tooth being pulled.

His prayer at the end of the chapter is the bravest in the book, because it admits fear:

“Father, I want to know Thee, but my coward heart fears to give up its toys. I cannot part with them without inward bleeding, and I do not try to hide from Thee the terror of the parting. I come trembling, but I do come. Please root from my heart all those things which I have cherished so long and which have become a very part of my living self, so that Thou mayest enter and dwell there without a rival.”

“I come trembling, but I do come.” That might be the most useful sentence you take from this chapter. Giving things to God doesn't mean throwing them away. Abraham kept Isaac. You may keep your phone, your sport, your music, your friends, your plans. The question is whether they hold you, or God does. Maybe there is one thing, a person, a dream, the way people see you, that you would really struggle to hand over. That's the one Tozer means.

One thing to do this week: write down, by name, the one thing you would find hardest to hand over to God. Then pray Tozer's words over it: “I come trembling, but I do come.” You don't have to feel brave. You just have to come.

study_questions.question: What does Tozer say the words “my” and “mine” reveal?
study_questions.answer: Our deep urge to possess. They are small words, but they show how things have moved into the place in our hearts that belongs to God.

study_questions.question: What did Abraham lose on the mountain, and what did he keep?
study_questions.answer: He kept Isaac and everything he owned. What he lost was his possessive grip: afterwards he had everything but possessed nothing.

study_questions.question: Why does Tozer say we should “name things and people by their names”?
study_questions.answer: Because surrender has to be specific. Vague promises don't touch the actual things and people our hearts are clinging to.

fields.title: The Opaque Veil
fields.body_html:
“Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus” — Hebrews 10:19 (KJV)

Tozer opens this chapter with a sentence written about sixteen hundred years ago by Augustine: “Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee.” God made us for himself, and nothing else fits. An old catechism agrees: “Man's chief End is to glorify God and enjoy Him forever.”

But people ran from God, like Adam hiding among the trees. God is everywhere, so we can't actually escape him. What we lost was his felt presence. Our life became “a life away from the Presence,” and that loss is “the cause of our unceasing restlessness.”

To show the way back, Tozer walks us through the tabernacle, the great tent where Israel worshipped in the wilderness. First came an outer courtyard with an altar. Then, through a curtain, the holy place, lit by a golden lampstand. Then, behind a second, thicker curtain, or veil, the Holy of Holies, where God's presence dwelt. Only the high priest could go in, once a year. When Jesus died, the Gospels say, that veil in the Temple was torn from top to bottom. The way into God's presence is now open to everyone. It is “more than a doctrine to be held, it is a life to be enjoyed every moment of every day.”

So why, Tozer asks, do so many Christians stay outside? “We sense that the call is for us, but still we fail to draw near, and the years pass and we grow old and tired in the outer courts of the tabernacle.” His answer is that there is another veil, one inside us. It is “the close-woven veil of the self-life which we have never truly acknowledged.”

He names its threads. “To be specific, the self-sins are these: self-righteousness, self-pity, self-confidence, self-sufficiency, self-admiration, self-love and a host of others like them.” And then the key line: “They are not something we do, they are something we are.”

These sins can live comfortably in church. Tozer had seen self-promotion in Christian leaders and was sad that it was so common it hardly got noticed. Self, he says, “can fight for the faith of the Reformers and preach eloquently the creed of salvation by grace.” It “seems actually to feed upon orthodoxy and is more at home in a Bible Conference than in a tavern.” He's warning that good religious activity is the perfect place for pride to hide. “Self is the opaque veil that hides the Face of God from us.”

You can't learn your way out of it. Only God can tear this veil, and Tozer won't pretend it is painless. “It is never fun to die.” Letting God deal with your self-pity or your need to be admired hurts, because that veil is part of you. But he doesn't stop at the pain: “There comes a moment when its work is finished and the suffering victim dies. After that is resurrection glory and power.” He ends with a prayer:

“Lord, how excellent are Thy ways, and how devious and dark are the ways of man. Show us how to die, that we may rise again to newness of life. Rend the veil of our self-life from the top down as Thou didst rend the veil of the Temple. We would draw near in full assurance of faith.”

Read that list again. Self-pity after a bad day. Self-admiration when the likes roll in. Self-righteousness when you compare yourself with someone who messed up. Self-sufficiency when you think you can handle everything alone. That is not a reason to despair. It is a reason to be honest.

fields.title: Taste and See
fields.body_html:
“O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.” — Psalm 34:8 (KJV)

What is God to you, really? Tozer says that for most people, “God is an inference, not a reality.” They reason that someone must have made the world: “He must be,” they say, “therefore we believe He is.” Others only know about God “by hearsay,” from parents or teachers. For others God is a vague idea, another word for goodness or beauty.

And Christians, Tozer admits, are often not much different. They pray “Our Father,” which means God is a person they can know. Yet “for millions of Christians, nevertheless, God is no more real than He is to the non-Christian. They go through life trying to love an ideal and be loyal to a mere principle.”

The Bible talks very differently. It uses the language of the senses. “O taste and see that the Lord is good.” “My sheep hear my voice.” “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Tozer's conclusion is that we have spiritual senses, ways of knowing God that work as truly as eyes and ears do with the physical world. When God gives new life, those senses wake up. So why do so many believers seem numb? “The answer is our chronic unbelief.”

Then comes one of the most beautiful sentences in the book: “A spiritual kingdom lies all about us, enclosing us, embracing us, altogether within reach of our inner selves, waiting for us to recognize it.” God is not far off. “God Himself is here waiting our response to His Presence.”

Tozer is careful to explain two words. The first is “reality.” Something real exists whether anyone is thinking about it or not. God is real like that; more real, in fact, than anything else. “The worshipping heart does not create its Object.” The second word is “reckon,” which means to count on something. And this is not the same as imagining. “Imagination is not faith.” Faith doesn't invent anything. “Faith creates nothing; it simply reckons upon that which is already there.” You are not being asked to pretend. You are being asked to count on what is true.

He has fun with clever thinkers who say nothing is really real and then live as if everything is. “Their ideas are brain-deep, not life-deep.” The plain person, by contrast, feels the wind and rain on his face and knows they are real.

So what's the problem? The visible world is loud. “The world of sense intrudes upon our attention day and night for the whole of our lifetime. It is clamorous, insistent and self-demonstrating.” Tozer wrote that in 1948. “The visible becomes the enemy of the invisible; the temporal, of the eternal.” We have trained ourselves to think only what we see counts. But “The spiritual is real.” And the spiritual world is not just somewhere we go after death: “It is not future, but present.” He ends with a short prayer:

“O God, quicken to life every power within me, that I may lay hold on eternal things. Open my eyes that I may see; give me acute spiritual perception; enable me to taste Thee and know that Thou art good. Make heaven more real to me than any earthly thing has ever been. Amen.”

Think about how much of your day is spent responding to things that demand attention: notifications, feeds, group chats, the next video. None of that is evil. But it is, in Tozer's word, “clamorous.” It shouts. God doesn't shout. He waits.

And notice what Tozer is not asking. He isn't asking you to work up a feeling, or picture God in your head until he seems real. That would be imagination. He's asking you to reckon: to act on what is already true. God is here, now, in your bedroom, on your bus, in the exam hall. “Every man must choose his world,” he says. Choosing doesn't make God real. It makes you awake to him.

One thing to do this week: take one fifteen-minute walk this week with no earbuds and your phone in your pocket. As you walk, tell God thank you for real things you can see, hear and feel. Then say, quietly, And you are here too. That is reckoning.

study_questions.answer: Imagination makes up pictures and tries to make them real. Faith “creates nothing”; it counts on what is already there.

fields.title: And I Knew It Not
fields.body_html:
“Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?” — Psalm 139:7 (KJV)

This chapter is built on one simple, enormous truth. What does it mean that God is everywhere? “It means simply that God is here. Wherever we are, God is here. There is no place, there can be no place, where He is not.”

Tozer doesn't mean that God and nature are the same thing. God is in his world but far above it, the Creator and not the creation. Yet he is near: “No point is nearer to God than any other point.” Your bedroom is exactly as close to God as a cathedral.

David tried to imagine running away from God and couldn't: “If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.” So, Tozer asks, why isn't everyone overwhelmed by this? Jacob gave the answer. Alone in the desert, running from his brother, he had a dream of God, woke up and said, “Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.” Tozer's comment: “That was his trouble, and it is ours. Men do not know that God is here. What a difference it would make if they knew.”

So God's presence and our awareness of it are two different things. Getting nearer to God isn't about distance. Tozer uses a picture from family life. A father might say, “I feel that my son is coming nearer to me as he gets older,” even though his son has lived in the same house all his life. He means they understand each other better. That is the nearness we need: “We need never shout across the spaces to an absent God. He is nearer than our own soul, closer than our most secret thoughts.”

Then a hard question: why do some people seem to find God in a way others don't? God has no favourites. “The difference lies not with God but with us.” The great saints were wildly different from each other, but they shared one thing, which he calls “spiritual receptivity,” an openness to God. “They differed from the average person in that when they felt the inward longing they did something about it.”

That openness, he says, isn't a fixed amount. “It may be increased by exercise or destroyed by neglect.” And here Tozer gets frank about the Christians of his own day. They wanted quick results: “We read our chapter, have our short devotions and rush away.” He saw shallow lives and a lot of entertainment in church. But he doesn't point the finger at others only. “No Christian is wholly free from blame. We have all contributed.” That includes him.

Instead of getting tangled in debates, he gives a promise to anyone who turns to God seriously: “the results will exceed anything he may have hoped in his leaner and weaker days.” Then he prays like a man who has just woken up, like Jacob:

“O God and Father, I repent of my sinful preoccupation with visible things. The world has been too much with me. Thou hast been here and I knew it not. I have been blind to Thy Presence. Open my eyes that I may behold Thee in and around me. For Christ's sake, Amen.”

God is just as present in the school corridor, the dinner table and the changing room as in church. You don't have to go somewhere special to be near him. You just have to wake up to him where you are.

And notice what Tozer says about practice. Openness to God is something like a muscle, or like learning an instrument. A thirty-second verse before you rush out is better than nothing, but what grows it is responding when you feel that pull: stopping, turning, paying attention. The saints weren't a different kind of person. They just did something about the longing.

One thing to do this week: choose three ordinary places you will be in this week, like a bus stop, the lunch queue or your bedroom. Each time you are there, pause for a moment and say Jacob's words in your head, changed so that they end the right way: Surely the LORD is in this place, and I know it.

study_questions.question: What does Tozer say the presence of God means “in direct Christian experience”?
study_questions.answer: Simply that God is here, wherever we are. There is no place where he is not.

study_questions.question: What was Jacob's problem, according to Tozer?
study_questions.answer: God was with him all along, but he didn't know it. He said, “Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.”

study_questions.question: What is “spiritual receptivity,” and how does it grow?
study_questions.answer: An openness and responsiveness to God. It grows by being exercised, by acting on the longing for God when we feel it, and shrinks when it is neglected.

fields.title: Lord, Teach Me to Listen
fields.body_html:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” — John 1:1 (KJV)

John calls Jesus “the Word.” Why? Tozer says a word is how you express what you think, so calling the Son of God the Word tells us that God is the kind of God who speaks. And not only in the past. “God is speaking. Not God spoke, but God is speaking. He is by His nature continuously articulate.”

This, he says, is how the world exists at all. “The briefest and only satisfying cosmogony is this: 'He spake and it was done.'” (A cosmogony is an account of how the universe began.) “In the beginning He spoke to nothing, and it became something.” All through Genesis 1 the pattern repeats: God said, and it was so.

The Bible is God's written Word, and Tozer treasures it. But it is alive because God is still speaking through it: “It is the present Voice which makes the written Word all-powerful. Otherwise it would lie locked in slumber within the covers of a book.”

He thinks God's voice reaches everyone, even people who have never opened a Bible. In Proverbs, wisdom is pictured as a woman calling out in the streets: “Unto you, O men, I call.” Then he adds a sad line: “The tragedy is that our eternal welfare depends upon our hearing, and we have trained our ears not to hear.”

When God spoke from heaven to Jesus, some bystanders explained it away. “It thundered,” they said. Tozer thinks we do the same. “We are more likely to explain than to adore.” And yet, he says, almost everyone has had moments that are hard to explain: “a sudden sense of loneliness, or a feeling of wonder or awe in the face of the universal vastness.” He suggests those moments may be God trying to get our attention.

He even guesses that every beautiful thing humans have made, music, poetry, art, is a faulty response to that voice. Then he admits it is only his own idea. “It is my own belief (and here I shall not feel bad if no one follows me).” And: “But you can be a good Christian and not accept my thesis.” Blunt as he is, Tozer knows the difference between the Bible and his own opinions.

What he is sure of is this: “The Voice of God is a friendly Voice.” The problem is noise. “Religion has accepted the monstrous heresy that noise, size, activity and bluster make a man dear to God.” But God still says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” So: get still, get alone, open your Bible. First you may sense only “a sound as of a Presence walking in the garden.” Then a voice. Then the words on the page become “warm and intimate and clear as the word of a dear friend.”

He wants us to read the Bible as “not only a book which was once spoken, but a book which is now speaking.” “Come at once to the open Bible expecting it to speak to you.” And he prays, sounding, in 1948, as if he lived today:

“Lord, teach me to listen. The times are noisy and my ears are weary with the thousand raucous sounds which continuously assault them. Give me the spirit of the boy Samuel when he said to Thee, 'Speak, for thy servant heareth.' Let me hear Thee speaking in my heart. Let me get used to the sound of Thy Voice, that its tones may be familiar when the sounds of earth die away and the only sound will be the music of Thy speaking Voice. Amen.”

If Tozer found 1948 noisy, imagine what he would make of a phone that buzzes a hundred times a day. “My ears are weary” might be the most relatable line in the book. And notice who he wants to be like: Samuel, a boy when God first called him.

One thing to do this week: put your phone in another room for ten minutes. Open your Bible to a short passage (1 Samuel 3 is a good one) and read it slowly, “expecting it to speak to you.” Write down one sentence that stood out, and ask God what he means by it.

study_questions.answer: That God didn't just speak once long ago and then go silent. It is his nature to speak, and he is still speaking, including through the Bible.

study_questions.question: What did the crowd mean when they said “It thundered”?
study_questions.answer: They explained away God's voice as a natural event. Tozer says we often do the same: we are quicker to explain than to worship.

study_questions.question: How does Tozer suggest we start hearing God?
study_questions.answer: By getting still and alone, ideally with an open Bible, and reading it expecting God to speak, as a friend would.

fields.body_html:
“Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith” — Hebrews 12:2 (KJV)

Imagine someone reading the Bible for the first time. Tozer says one thing would quickly jump out: faith matters enormously. “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” So it is natural to ask, “What is faith?” And straight after that, the scary question: “Do I have faith?”

Most answers don't impress Tozer. Some teachers tell stories of answered prayers for health or money. Others pile on philosophy, “paring the slender hair of faith thinner and thinner till it disappears.” The Bible hardly defines faith; it shows faith in action. As he puts it, borrowing an old saying: “I had rather exercise faith than know the definition thereof.”

So he goes to a story. In Numbers 21, the Israelites complained against God in the desert, and poisonous snakes came among them. “And they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.” God told Moses to make a bronze snake and lift it up on a pole: “everyone that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.” Centuries later Jesus pointed to that very story: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”

fields.title: Be Thou Exalted
fields.body_html:
“Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens; let thy glory be above all the earth.” — Psalm 57:5 (KJV)

Everything works when it is in the right place, and Tozer says the same is true of people. Our deepest trouble is “a radical moral dislocation,” like a shoulder out of its socket. We are out of place with God. “Essentially salvation is the restoration of a right relation between man and his Creator.”

To know where you stand, you need a fixed point. God is that point. When God gave his name to Moses, he called himself “I AM.” Tozer loves this: “When He speaks in the first person He says, 'I AM'; when we speak of Him we say, 'He is'; when we speak to Him we say, 'Thou art.'”

Then he offers a test. Most people say God is first. But put them in a real choice, “between God and money, between God and men, between God and personal ambition, God and self, God and human love, and God will take second place every time.” It's not what we say that shows who is on top. It's what we choose, day after day.

The answer is in three words from the Psalms: “Be thou exalted.” Tozer calls it “a little key to unlock the door to great treasures of grace.” Once you really mean it, “a thousand minor problems will be solved at once.”

Does putting God first make you smaller? No. “In exalting God over all he finds his own highest honor upheld.” Everyone serves something. Jesus said, “Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.” The choice is between “a cruel slave driver” and “a kind and gentle Master whose yoke is easy.”

God once told the priest Eli, “Them that honour me I will honour.” Eli's sons did not, and the story ended in tragedy: they were killed in battle and Eli fell and died. Against them Tozer sets people like Abraham and David, who tried to honour God with all their flaws. “Not perfection, but holy intention made the difference.”

Jesus once asked, “How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God alone?” Tozer thinks wanting people's approval can make faith impossible. And he admits one fear: “it is that I may convince the mind before God can win the heart.” You can agree with all of this and still not do it. “God wants us all, and He will not rest till He gets us all.” So he prays, line by line, over every part of his life:

“O God, be Thou exalted over my possessions. Nothing of earth's treasures shall seem dear unto me if only Thou art glorified in my life. Be Thou exalted over my friendships. I am determined that Thou shalt be above all, though I must stand deserted and alone in the midst of the earth. Be Thou exalted above my comforts. Though it mean the loss of bodily comforts and the carrying of heavy crosses I shall keep my vow made this day before Thee. Be Thou exalted over my reputation. Make me ambitious to please Thee even if as a result I must sink into obscurity and my name be forgotten as a dream. Rise, O Lord, into Thy proper place of honor, above my ambitions, above my likes and dislikes, above my family, my health and even my life itself. Let me decrease that Thou mayest increase, let me sink that Thou mayest rise above.”

That is a costly prayer, and Tozer wants us to mean “everything we say.” “Over my friendships” might be the hardest line for you. So might “my reputation,” or “my ambitions.” That's fine. Pray the lines you can mean today, and tell God honestly which ones you can't pray yet. Holy intention, Tozer says, is what God looks at.

One thing to do this week: take one line of Tozer's prayer each day this week: possessions, friendships, comforts, reputation, ambitions, family. Each morning, pray that one line and ask what it would look like for God to be first in that area today.

fields.title: Pretty Small Stuff
fields.body_html:
“Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.” — Matthew 5:5 (KJV)

Want a description of the human race? Tozer says take the Beatitudes, Jesus' list of who is blessed, and turn them inside out. “Instead of poverty of spirit we find the rankest kind of pride; instead of mourners we find pleasure seekers; instead of meekness, arrogance.” Instead of peacemakers, people “quarrelsome and resentful.” And it makes us miserable. “Pride, arrogance, resentfulness, evil imaginings, malice, greed: these are the sources of more human pain than all the diseases that ever afflicted mortal flesh.”

Jesus wasn't guessing. “He is not offering an opinion; Jesus never uttered opinions. He never guessed; He knew, and He knows.”

Jesus explained what “meek” meant later in Matthew: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart.” The burden Jesus means, Tozer says, is inside us. And rest is not another thing to achieve: “It is not something we do, it is what comes to us when we cease to do.”

The first burden is pride. “Think for yourself whether much of your sorrow has not arisen from someone speaking slightingly of you.” Tozer describes people “smarting under each fancied slight, tossing sleepless if another is preferred before them.”

The meek person handles it with humour, talking to himself like this: “Oh, so you have been overlooked? They have placed someone else before you? They have whispered that you are pretty small stuff after all? And now you feel hurt because the world is saying about you the very things you have been saying about yourself?” And then: “Come on, humble yourself, and cease to care what men think.”

Meekness is not weakness. “The meek man is not a human mouse afflicted with a sense of his own inferiority.” He may be “as bold as a lion and as strong as Samson.” He knows he is weak on his own, but he also knows that “he is in the sight of God of more importance than angels.” Tozer gives him a motto: “In himself, nothing; in God, everything.” So he stops defending himself. “He will be happy to let God defend him.”

The second burden is pretending. “The fear of being found out gnaws like rodents within their hearts.” The rich man fears his clothes or his car will look cheap next to someone else's. Advertising, he says, plays “continually upon this desire to appear what we are not.” Little children, by contrast, “do not compare; they receive direct enjoyment from what they have.” Comparison comes later, and so does envy.

Jesus offers rest from all of it, “the blessed relief which comes when we accept ourselves for what we are and cease to pretend.” And we don't carry it alone. “He calls it 'my yoke,' and He walks at one end while we walk at the other.” Tozer's prayer is short and childlike:

“Lord, make me childlike. Deliver me from the urge to compete with another for place or prestige or position. I would be simple and artless as a little child. Deliver me from pose and pretense. Forgive me for thinking of myself. Help me to forget myself and find my true peace in beholding Thee. That Thou mayest answer this prayer I humble myself before Thee. Lay upon me Thy easy yoke of self-forgetfulness that through it I may find rest. Amen.”

You probably know these burdens well. Not being picked. Being left out of the group chat. Seeing everyone else's best moments on your screen and quietly ranking yourself against them. Editing how you look before anyone sees you. That's exhausting, and you were never meant to carry it. Meekness doesn't mean hating yourself; it means you matter so much to God that you can stop needing everyone else to agree.

One thing to do this week: the next time you feel overlooked or left out, try Tozer's trick: answer yourself with a bit of kind humour, then tell God, You can defend me. I'm putting this down. And for one week, post or send nothing whose main purpose is to make you look better than you are.

study_questions.question: What does Tozer say the human race looks like?
study_questions.answer: Like the Beatitudes turned inside out: pride instead of poverty of spirit, arrogance instead of meekness, quarrelling instead of peacemaking.

study_questions.question: Is meekness the same as weakness or low self-esteem?
study_questions.answer: No. The meek person can be “as bold as a lion.” He knows he is nothing in himself but everything in God, so he stops defending himself and lets God do it.

study_questions.question: What is the “burden of pretense”?
study_questions.answer: The constant effort to look better than we are and the fear of being found out. Jesus offers rest from it when we accept ourselves as we are and stop pretending.

fields.title: The Whole World a Sanctuary
fields.body_html:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.” — 1 Corinthians 10:31 (KJV)

Tozer's last chapter tackles a hidden problem. We split life into two boxes. One box is “sacred”: praying, reading the Bible, singing, going to church. The other box is “secular”: “eating, sleeping, working, looking after the needs of the body.” The second we do “reluctantly,” sometimes “apologizing to God for what we consider a waste of time and strength.” The result? People “try to walk the tight rope between two kingdoms and they find no peace in either.”

Tozer thinks the split is false. Jesus said, “I do always the things that please him.” Paul told Christians to do everything to the glory of God, and he deliberately mentioned eating and drinking, the most ordinary things there are. “If these lowly animal acts can be so performed as to honor God, then it becomes difficult to conceive of one that cannot.” (Sin, Tozer is clear, can never honour God; he means ordinary, good things.)

So for someone who has given their life to God, “every act of his life is or can be as truly sacred as prayer or baptism or the Lord's Supper.” Everything is lifted up. The answer, when old habits nag, is to offer every part of the day to God and believe he accepts it, with “a thousand thought-prayers as we go about the job of living.”

The same goes for places. God once taught Israel holiness through holy days and a holy tent, but Jesus said true worshippers would worship “in spirit and in truth.” Tozer then criticises the Roman Catholic church, and his own Fundamentalist circles too, for treating certain days and places as holier than others, such as “Lent” and “holy week.” He says he speaks “in all charity.” Many sincere Christians, Catholic and Protestant, keep those seasons gladly, and you don't have to agree with him there to take his main point: God can be met anywhere.

Not everything is equally important. “Paul's sewing of tents was not equal to his writing of an Epistle to the Romans, but both were accepted of God.” And: “the planting of the garden can be as holy an act as the winning of a soul.” What makes the difference? “It is not what a man does that determines whether his work is sacred or secular, it is why he does it. The motive is everything.” For such a person, “living itself will be sacramental and the whole world a sanctuary.”

His final prayer gathers the whole book together: trust, surrender, possessing nothing, the Presence, the Voice, rest, and every act as worship:

“Lord, I would trust Thee completely; I would be altogether Thine; I would exalt Thee above all. I desire that I may feel no sense of possessing anything outside of Thee. I want constantly to be aware of Thy overshadowing Presence and to hear Thy speaking Voice. I long to live in restful sincerity of heart. I want to live so fully in the Spirit that all my thought may be as sweet incense ascending to Thee and every act of my life may be an act of worship.”

One honest word about Tozer himself. His biographers do not hide that his hunger for God made him distant from his wife and seven children. His own last chapter points the better way: time with your family is not a distraction from God but part of worshipping him. Tozer died in Toronto on 12 May 1963 and was buried in Akron, Ohio, under a simple stone that calls him A Man of God. That is a good thing to be called. Be one at the dinner table too.

Your Tuesday counts. Homework, training, washing up, listening to a friend who is struggling: done for God, it is as holy as anything you do on a Sunday. God is waiting in the middle of your ordinary life.

One thing to do this week: pick the most boring task you have this week, like a chore, a revision session or a long journey. Before you start, say to God, This is for you. Then do it well. Afterwards, go back to the sentence you wrote at the start of this book and see whether it has changed.

study_questions.question: What is the “sacred-secular” split?
study_questions.answer: Dividing life into holy activities like prayer and church, and ordinary ones like eating, working and sleeping, and feeling that only the first kind pleases God.

study_questions.question: According to Tozer, what makes ordinary work sacred?
study_questions.answer: The motive. “It is not what a man does... it is why he does it.” Work done for God is worship.

study_questions.question: What does Tozer's last prayer gather together?
study_questions.answer: The whole book: trusting God, being entirely his, exalting him above all, possessing nothing outside him, knowing his Presence, hearing his Voice, living without pretending, and making every act worship.

Tozer died in Toronto on 12 May 1963 and was buried in Akron, Ohio, under a simple stone that calls him A Man of God. That is a good thing to be called. Be one at the dinner table too. Your Tuesday counts. Homework, training, washing up, listening to a friend who is struggling: done for God, it is as holy as anything you do on a Sunday. God is waiting in the middle of your ordinary life. One thing to do this week: pick the most boring task you have this week, like a chore, a revision session or a long journey. Before you start, say to God, This is for you. Then do it well. Afterwards, go back to the sentence you wrote at the start of this book and see whether it has changed.
